prompt: A IPv4 datagram contains \(4\,000\,\mathrm{byte}\) IP payload and a 20 byte header without options. On a link with MTU 1,500, the payload is divided into 1,480, 1,480 and \(1\,040\,\mathrm{byte}\). How many bytes are sent at IP level for the three fragments?
explanation: Each fragment gets its own 20 byte IP header. Totally, it's going to be \(4\,000 + 3\cdot 20 = 4\,060\,\mathrm{byte}\). Compared to the unfragmented datagram, this is the 40 extra header change.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 18–20

prompt: A path has IP-MTU 1,500, 9,000 and \(1\,280\,\mathrm{byte}\) on the three links. You will send one UDP datagram without fragmentation. Assume 20-byte IPv4-header without options, 8-byte UDP-header and no tunnels. What is the maximum UDP usage?
explanation: The path constraint is the smallest MTU, \(1\,280\,\mathrm{byte}\). Both headers must be accommodated: \(1\,280-20-8 = 1\,252\,\mathrm{byte}\). The big MTU on the middle link does not increase the path's minimum.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 18–22

prompt: Two unlimited large flows hashes to the same path on an ECMP network with two otherwise open roads on \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) each. Each flow is kept on its chosen path, and the hash choice is not changed. What limits the overall rate of the two floats in this situation?

options.text: The rate is determined only by RTT, not by the link capacity

explanation: Per-flow distribution can place several large flows on the same path. They then compete for \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) while the other way is unused. ECMP does not automatically give equal byte distribution.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 27–33

prompt: Packet A is sent by \(t=0\,\mathrm{ms}\) via a road with \(30\,\mathrm{ms}\) delay. Packet B is sent by \(t=5\,\mathrm{ms}\) via another route with \(10\,\mathrm{ms}\) delay. No packets are lost or delayed in line. What does the recipient observe?

options.text: A and B come at the same time

explanation: A arrives at \(30\,\mathrm{ms}\) and B at \(5+10=15\,\mathrm{ms}\). B thus comes \(15\,\mathrm{ms}\) before A. Different road delay is enough to create reorganise, without package loss.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 24–30

prompt: A TCP flow held on one of two ECMP routes is automatically given the sum of the capacity of both roads.
explanation: When the entire flow is kept on one road, it is this road’s capacity that is available to it. That other flows can use a different path does not mean that one float uses both.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 27–33

prompt: A path MTU found once remains valid after all route changes as long as the sender's own network card has unchanged MTU.
explanation: The Path MTU depends on all the links on the current path. A new route may contain a link with a lower MTU than the old one.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 18–22

prompt: A protocol detects that a PDU has the wrong checksum and rejects it, but does nothing more. What function is demonstrated and what is missing to restore data with ARQ?

options.text: Flow control is done; new receiver credit will recreate content
Duplicate detection has been performed; copy number two must be rejected
Bug detection done; a retransmission mechanism is needed
Bug correction complete; original successfully recreated

explanation: Detecting and rejecting corrupt data is not the same as restoring them. ARQ uses feedback or timeout to get a new copy sent.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 56–65

prompt: A receiver delivers a PDU, but its ACK is lost. The sender retransmits the PDU. What prevents duplicate delivery to the upper layer?

options.text: Increasing the maximum size of each transmitted data unit
Acknowledging every retransmission without inspecting its identity
Recalculating the route whenever an acknowledgment is lost
Detecting duplicates using identifiers or sequence information

explanation: The receiver needs to recognize that a retransmitted PDU was already delivered. Identifiers or sequence numbers distinguish duplicates from genuinely new data.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 60–65

prompt: A service shall be able to communicate with both a local and a remote process through the same interface. What should the application ideally fail to choose for itself?

options.text: The physical connection or interface used
Whether a response is correct for the application
Whether to send a new application

explanation: Communication service may hide the selection of local connection and physical interface. This provides the same service interface, but does not guarantee identical latency or faultless application logic.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 48–54

prompt: A communicates with D via B and C. Each of the three individual links has one local fault control loop, and A-D has one separate control loop over the whole path. How many control loops and scope are specified in the model?

options.text: Six, because each link has to be counted twice
Four control loops: three link ranges and one A–D range
One, because all incorrect checks must be on the same layer
Three, because the A-D control is the same instance as the link control

explanation: The three links each have their own state and their own range of communication. In addition, the end-to-end loop covers the whole A-D path. Equal function at different levels is not the same control body.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 78–87

prompt: On a dedicated point-to-point link with exactly one neighbour, output interfaces can only identify the receiving neighbour; a shared medium may require addresses to select from among several neighbours.
explanation: The notes distinguish between one wire and one neighbour and multi-access. A local interface selects the neighbour of the first type, while for example MAC addresses separate the recipients from a shared medium.

prompt: Node H has two links. One fails, but routing finds a path through the other. What advantage does a node-based identity provide?

options.text: Every interface must share the same link-layer address.
Packets on the failed link are recovered without retransmission.
No node needs a forwarding table after the path changes.
The destination keeps its identity while its reachable path changes.

explanation: A node identity can be stable across interfaces and new paths. This is separate from restoring lost packets or finding the actual path.

prompt: An application uses a transport interface such as TAPS and specifies a service name rather than locking to one IP address. What choice will be easier to leave to the transport system?

options.text: Selecting from available service addresses and paths
Determines whether the user's password is correct
Determination of the content of all application responses
Removing the Need for Congestion Control

explanation: The name-based binding allows the transport to select or change the underlying addresses and paths. The name does not determine the application's own authentication rules or response.

prompt: If a recipient ignores reserved header fields, senders can in principle use these fields as a hidden channel even if the normal protocol processing works.
explanation: The notes point out that tolerance for reserved fields can have this backside. The fact that the normal recipient ignores a field does not prevent two cooperating parties from reading and writing additional information there.

prompt: An MPTCP connection has two subflows that share a bottleneck with one regular TCP connection. What goal motivates coupled congestion control over two independent, equally aggressive TCP controllers?

options.text: Make both subflows use the same rate even on different bottlenecks.
Let the faster subflow ignore congestion experienced by the slower one.
Avoid taking two flows' share at a bottleneck shared with one TCP flow.
Let both subflows compete independently as two ordinary TCP flows.

explanation: Coupling seeks to prevent multiple subflows from giving an MPTCP connection an unfair aggregate advantage at a shared bottleneck. When paths differ, it can also shift traffic towards the less congested path.

prompt: A protocol reproduces a connection identifier while old PDUs may still be on the way. What problem must configuration and synchronization handle?

options.text: That all new PDUs necessarily get too big MTU
That old and new connection must use different physical cables
That checksum cannot be calculated when returning ports
That old PDUs may be taken for data in the new connection

explanation: The state of the new connection must be distinguishable from delayed data in a former instance. This is a reason for coordinating the configuration, sequence information and service life of the condition.
source: IN3230 course introduction and repetition · Paragraphs 61–66

prompt: Sender 's timestamp increases once per milliseconds. A segment has timestamp 12,400. An ACK that unambiguously reflects this segment is received when the same sender clock shows 12,468. The receiver clock will fail 5 seconds. What is the RTT test?

options.text: It cannot be measured without synchronised clocks

explanation: The time stamp is reflected unchanged, and both times come from the transmitter's clock: \(12\,468-12\,400=68\,\mathrm{ms}\). The receiver's clock deviation is not included in this difference.

prompt: A sender gets DSACK for byte it has recently returned. What conclusion is directly supported by DSACK information?

options.text: The sender's first timeout must have been too short in all cases
Recipients have observed overlapping or duplicated data
The network must be completely free of packet reordering
Both copies must have taken the same route

explanation: DSACK reports duplicate data in the recipient. It may help to detect unnecessary retransmissions, but the report alone does not determine all the cause details or the route that the copies took.

prompt: During loss repair, the transmitter stops long and then sends a large brush. What idea in the notes is specifically aimed at allocating the consignments more evenly during recovery?

options.text: Increasing initial window on each duplicate ACK

explanation: The PRR and the precursor rate-halfing regulate transmission during recovery. The purpose in this context is to avoid the described combination of break and dense brush.

prompt: Use the simplified RTOR rule in the lecture: the hour will be restarted using \(\mathrm{RTO}-t\), where \(t\) is time since the current outstanding transmission. RTO is \(240\,\mathrm{ms}\) and an ACK comes after \(70\,\mathrm{ms}\). How much remaining wait with RTOR, and how much later would a full restart on \(240\,\mathrm{ms}\) trigger timeout?

options.text: \(240\,\mathrm{ms}\) remaining; full restart would be \(170\,\mathrm{ms}\) later
\(70\,\mathrm{ms}\) remaining; full restart would be \(240\,\mathrm{ms}\) later
\(170\,\mathrm{ms}\) remaining; full restart would be \(70\,\mathrm{ms}\) later

explanation: RTOR sets the specified remaining time to \(240-70=170\,\mathrm{ms}\). A restart with the entire \(240\,\mathrm{ms}\) from ACK time extends the wait with \(70\,\mathrm{ms}\).

prompt: A service will send ‘load card with 100 kr’ as early data in TCP Fast Open. The operation has no duplicate protection. What is the risk that the application design has to address?

options.text: That early data may be processed more than once by repeated SYN
That TCP necessarily changes the amount of another number
That a TFO cookie automatically makes the payment operation idempotent
That the server cannot send a response after SYN

explanation: TCP Fast Open can deliver data early. A cookie does not make the application action idempotent. A unique operation ID and duplicate detection can help protect the action.

prompt: In a simplified slow-start model, regular ACK counts increase \(\mathit{cwnd}\) by \(1\,\mathrm{MSS}\) per ACK. ABC increases instead by the number of newly signed MSS, not more than 2 per ACK. Four ACKs each receive 2 new MSS. How much does \(\mathit{cwnd}\) increase in total by the two rules?
explanation: The normal count is \(4\cdot 1=4\,\mathrm{MSS}\). The given ABC rule returns \(4\cdot\min(2,2)=8\,\mathrm{MSS}\). The difference is because each delayed ACK covers more than one segment.

prompt: Use the simplified RCK criteria of the lecture: an unmatched packet is considered to be lost when a packet sent at least \(\mathit{reo\_wnd}\) later is acknowledged. \(\mathit{reo\_wnd}=5\,\mathrm{ms}\). A is sent by \(0\,\mathrm{ms}\), B by \(3\,\mathrm{ms}\) and C by \(8\,\mathrm{ms}\). Only C's signed. Which packets meet this criterion?

options.text: None until three duplicate ACKs arrive

explanation: C sent \(8\,\mathrm{ms}\) after A and \(5\,\mathrm{ms}\) after B. Both differences are at least \(5\,\mathrm{ms}\). The task uses the explicitly simplified time criterion, not a claim for full implementation logic.

prompt: An established TCP connection shall send a response to \(6\,\mathrm{MSS}\). Assume that no data are outstanding, no packets are lost, that the receiving window is at least \(10\,\mathrm{MSS}\), and that \(\mathit{cwnd}\) is equal to the initial window. Compare \(\mathrm{IW}=4\,\mathrm{MSS}\) and \(\mathrm{IW}=10\,\mathrm{MSS}\). How many MSSs can be sent before the first ACK with each setting?

options.text: IW 4 sends 6 MSS; IW 10 sends 6 MSS.
IW 4 sends 4 MSS; IW 10 sends 10 MSS.
IW 4 sends 1 MSS; IW 10 sends 1 MSS.
IW 4 sends 4 MSS; IW 10 sends 6 MSS.

explanation: Outstanding data is limited by the window, but transmission also requires available application data. IW 4 permits 4 of the 6 MSS before ACKs; IW 10 permits all 6.

prompt: An advertised TCP receiver window at zero is only proof that a route queue in the network is full.
explanation: The receiving window is flow control and relates to the capacity of the recipient. It can be zero even if the network is not overloaded.

prompt: The TCP time stamp option can provide better RTT information without using space in the segment header.
explanation: The option is included in the header and thus uses space. The notes mention extra header space as a cost of the mechanism.

prompt: A packet arrives behind 80 packets on \(1\,500\,\mathrm{byte}\) in a FIFO queue. The link sends with \(12\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\). Assume that no packet has already been partially sent, and ignore new arrivals and headers. How long must the packet wait before sending itself?
explanation: The 80 packets form \(80\cdot 1\,500\cdot 8=960\,000\,\mathrm{bit}\). The waiting time will be \(\frac{960\,000}{12\,000\,000}\,\mathrm{s}=0.08\,\mathrm{s}=80\,\mathrm{ms}\). Your own transmission time is not included.

prompt: Networks A and B both have mean one-way delay 20 ms. A stays near 20 ms; B alternates between 5 and 35 ms. What follows?

options.text: B has a lower average delay because some samples are 5 ms.
A has greater packet loss because its delay stays near 20 ms.
The equal average delay implies that both have equal jitter.
B has greater jitter because its individual delays vary more.

explanation: Both networks have mean delay 20 ms. B's measurements fluctuate more around that mean, so it has greater delay variation, or jitter.

prompt: A schedule that gives each flow equal proportion necessarily gives each user equal to the total share, even when users create a different number of flows.
explanation: Justice per float is not the same as justice per user. A user with multiple simultaneous flows can receive multiple shares.

prompt: Use the CoDel model in the notes: minimum queue delay must be above \(5\,\mathrm{ms}\) through a full range of \(100\,\mathrm{ms}\) to trigger dropping state. A has constant \(6\,\mathrm{ms}\) in \(120\,\mathrm{ms}\). B has \(20\,\mathrm{ms}\) in \(40\,\mathrm{ms}\) and then \(1\,\mathrm{ms}\). What case does the described persistent condition meet?

options.text: Both, because both have had above \(5\,\mathrm{ms}\)

explanation: A remains above the goal in more than a full 100-ms interval. B falls below the goal after \(40\,\mathrm{ms}\). CoDel's looking for continuous queues, not just one high sample.

prompt: When queues are selected with a hash of the float's femur, two different flows can in principle be in the same queue.
explanation: A hash has a final number of possible queue indices, and different inputs may impact. "Per float" describes the objective of the breakdown, not a mathematical guarantee against all hash collisions.

prompt: A large, timeless system update shall provide for interactive traffic on the same access link. What idea from the notes is particularly appropriate to this goal?

options.text: Increasing the transmission rate every time RTT increases
Opening as much as possible independent aggressive flows
A low priority regulator such as LEDBAT

explanation: LEDBAT is motivated by background traffic to accommodate others. It's a different goal from maximizing your own proportion independently of other applications.

prompt: A test model uses \(\mathit{cwnd}_{\text{new}}=0.8\cdot\mathit{cwnd}\) for ECN marks and \(0.5\cdot\mathit{cwnd}\) for package losses. Both signals occur separately from \(\mathit{cwnd}=50\,\mathrm{MSS}\). What difference in a new window gives the model?

options.text: ECN provides \(50\,\mathrm{MSS}\) because the packet appeared

explanation: \(0.8\cdot 50=40\) and \(0.5\cdot 50=25\), so the difference is \(15\,\mathrm{MSS}\). The factors are the problem's example, not universal TCP constants. ABE illustrates that ECN and losses can justify different reductions.

prompt: If an application only provides \(2\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\) data and everything comes with \(2\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\), the measurement alone shows that the maximum capacity of the path is \(2\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\).
explanation: The measurement may be limited by the traffic offered. Capacity estimation must distinguish application limitations from a rate that flattens because the network is fully exploited.

prompt: Three flows share one 12-Mbit/s link after max-min justice. A needs a maximum of \(2\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\), B a maximum of \(7\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\), and C has unlimited needs. No other restrictions apply. What assignment does \((A,\,B,\,C)\) fill the link fairly?
explanation: First all increase equally to A when 2. The remaining \(10\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\) is equal to B and C. So 5 is equal to each. A doesn't need any more, and B and C have equal, limited shares.

prompt: Two flows have rates 12 and \(4\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\). In a simplified AIMD model both increase first by \(2\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\), and at the next common overload signal both halves the rate. What are the rates and the difference after these two steps?
explanation: Additive increase results in 14 and 6, and halving results in 7 and 3. The absolute difference was 8 before the reduction and becomes 4 afterwards. The model illustrates one common AIMD round.

prompt: A satellite PEP transparently buffers TCP data and processes ACKs to repair losses locally. What changes when the traffic uses QUIC with protected transport information?

options.text: Protected transport state prevents the same transparent ACK processing.
QUIC removes IP addresses from every packet's externally visible header.
QUIC requires a complete response to fit inside one UDP datagram.
QUIC delegates all loss recovery to intermediate satellite equipment.

explanation: Protected QUIC transport information prevents a transparent intermediary from inspecting and manipulating ACK state as it did with TCP. QUIC itself still implements loss recovery.

prompt: A \(12\,\mathrm{Mbit}\) video segment must be delivered every 4 seconds. An unpaced sender transmits at \(12\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\) for 1 second, then stays idle for 3 seconds. What constant rate delivers the same amount of data every 4 seconds if overhead is ignored?
explanation: The average need is \(\frac{12\,\mathrm{Mbit}}{4\,\mathrm{s}}=3\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\). A smooth 3-Mbit/s stream provides the same volume with less burstiness, provided this delivery plan fits the playback buffer.

prompt: A radio transmitter represents the bit values with two carrier waves of the same frequency and amplitude, but the phases 0 and \(\pi\). Which modulation is described?
explanation: Two discrete phases with otherwise similar frequency and amplitude are binary phase shift modulation. ASK varies amplitude and FSK uses different frequencies.

prompt: In a synchronous CDMA model, code \(A=(1,\,1,\,-1,\,-1)\) and code \(B=(1,\,1,\,1,\,-1)\) are used. What does the inner product tell us about these codes?

options.text: The inner product is 0; they are orthogonal
The inner product is 4; they are identical
The inner product is −4; they are opposite
The inner product is 2; they are not orthogonal

explanation: \(A\cdot B=1+1-1+1=2\). Therefore, the cross-submission does not disappear in the ideal correlation decoder, as it would for orthogonal codes.

prompt: That two chips sequences have an internal product zero when properly adjusted, guarantees that the inner product is still zero at any relative time shift.
explanation: Orthogonality applies to the compared adjusted sequences. A time shift changes what chip values are multiplied, and zero by one adjustment does not guarantee zero by all.

prompt: Use \(\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}}=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{S}{N}\right)\) and \(C=B\log_2\left(1+\frac{S}{N}\right)\). A non-profit channel has a bandwidth of \(B=1\,\mathrm{MHz}\) and \(\mathrm{SNR}=20\,\mathrm{dB}\). What capacity limit does it have? Use \(\log_2 (101)\approx 6.66\) and \(\log_2 (21)\approx 4.39\).
explanation: \(20\,\mathrm{dB}\) means linear \(\frac{S}{N}=10^{\frac{20}{10}}=100\). This means \(C=1\,000\,000\cdot\log_2(101)\approx6.66\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\). Setting 20 directly as the linear ratio results in an incorrect \(4.39\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\).

prompt: An FDMA system has given each of four users a fixed equal frequency band. One user is active and three are silent. The allocation does not change. What is the consequence for the active user?

options.text: It must wait for a separate slot before each shipment
It has to switch to the same chip code as the other three.
It cannot automatically use the reserved bands of the three others
It automatically gets all bandwidth through the FDMA definition

explanation: Fixed frequency allocation separates users by bands. The fact that others are quiet does not in itself transfer the rights of these bands; it would require a modified allocation mechanism.

prompt: A \(4\times 4\)-MIMO connection has four transmitter and four receiver antennas. In a simplified model, the channel of rank 1 is, and the maximum number of independent data streams is \(\min\)(the number of transmit antennas, the number of receiving antennas, the range). What is the limit?
explanation: The specified limit is \(\min(4,4,1)=1\). Several antennas do not provide four independent flows when the ducts do not provide the necessary independent spatial dimensions.

prompt: Two channels with equal bandwidth and equal to linear \(\frac{S}{N}\) get the same Shannon-Hartley limit, although the carrier frequencies are different.
explanation: The reported capacity model includes bandwidth and \(\frac{S}{N}\), not carrier frequency directly. In practice, higher frequency can provide access to wider bands, but it is kept equal here.

prompt: A measurement shows several delayed copies of exactly the same radio symbol from one transmitter. The copies follow different reflection paths. What's the most direct explanation?

options.text: A TDMA schedule that assigns multiple users the same slot
An error in the IP Address Allocation

explanation: Reflections may signal the same signal along different routes with different journey times. It's multipath, and it doesn't require multiple independent transmitters to compete.

prompt: A hears B transmitting and defers under CSMA. Measurements show their transmissions would not interfere at either receiver. What does this illustrate?

options.text: A is hidden because it can hear B's carrier transmission.
A needs a larger TCP receive window before using the channel.
Carrier sensing can defer transmissions that would not interfere.
Carrier sensing reveals interference at every possible receiver exactly.

explanation: Carrier sensing measures the channel at the transmitter, while interference matters at the receivers. Under these conditions, deferral is unnecessarily conservative: the exposed-terminal problem.

prompt: A receipt for a local wireless link transfer is not only a confirmation that a remote application has received and processed the content.
explanation: Local link control and end-to-end communications differ in scope. A packet may continue to be lost or wait for subsequent links, and application management requires its own assumptions.

prompt: A simplified model compares the waste airtime per experiment. Without RTS/CTS, the wallpaper is \(p\cdot2\,000\,\mu\mathrm{s}\), where \(p\) is the collision probability. With reservation, the cost is always \(100\,\mu\mathrm{s}\), and the model assumes no losses beyond this. For which \(p\) has reservation lower expected cost?
explanation: Reservation is better when \(100<p\cdot2\,000\), i.e. \(p>\frac{100}{2\,000}=0.05\). This is an explicitly idealed balance between reservation cost and long collisions, not a full Wi-Fi model.

prompt: In a simple model, two transmitters choose independently and uniformly one of the 0, 1, 2 or 3 slots after the channel becomes free. Collision means they pick the same hatch. What is the probability of collision in this choice?
explanation: There are \(4\cdot 4=16\) equally likely pairs. Four pairs have the same hatch: \((0,\,0)\), \((1,\,1)\), \((2,\,2)\) and \((3,\,3)\). The probability is \(\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}\).

prompt: A laptop is authenticated and associated with an access point, but does not get any IP configuration. What distinction is important in the debugging?

options.text: DHCP must be finished before Beacons can be received
Missing IP address proves that the radio transmitter has been rejected
Wi-Fi connection and IP configuration are separate steps
Success association proves that DNS already works

explanation: The notes distinguish association from the subsequent typical DHCP process. You should examine the IP configuration without assuming that all local radio connections have thus failed.

prompt: A telephone that roams in another country may use radio resources, while at the same time having user traffic transmitted via the core network of the home country.
explanation: This is just the distinction between visited radio networks and home-routed user traffic. The GTP tunnel can go to P-GW on its home network even if the radio is connected locally.

prompt: An operator considers local breakout to reduce roaming latency. Which operational trade-off matters?

options.text: A shorter data path trades off against charging, control and troubleshooting.
A shorter data path requires slower radio modulation in the visited network.
A shorter data path removes all need to coordinate between the operators.
A shorter data path guarantees simpler charging and fault attribution.

explanation: Home routing provides the home operator with an overall traffic point and easier access to billing information. A shorter data route may be attractive, but organisational and operational conditions affect the choice.

prompt: Two mobile subscriptions use the same radio base station, but receive different rates and different roaming delay. What explanation is technically reasonable without assuming measurement errors?

options.text: Radio base station alone decides all the way to the application server
Subscription policy and further core network routing may differ
Equal base station makes all end-to-end performance identical
Equal signal strength guarantees the same priority in the core network

explanation: The radio resources are only one part of the way. Service and subscriber policies may affect the rate, but, among other things, the roaming procedure may affect delay.

prompt: A provider describes a product as cloud computing. The customer must reserve fixed capacity for a year at a time and pays the same at zero and full usage. Which core cloud computing characteristic does this description support least?

options.text: That services may have a documented level of quality

explanation: Utility computing is about resources when needed and payment related to use. The product name alone doesn't say that this particular price model meets the idea.

prompt: Therefore, when a cloud solution is scalable, it automatically adjusts capacity up and down with the current load.
explanation: Scalability and elasticity are related, but elasticity focuses on dynamic adaptation. A capacity may be possible to increase even if manual planning is required.

prompt: A service requires both front end and database access. Each is available with probability 0.99 at any time and the error modes are assumed to be independent. What is the availability of the service in this model?
explanation: Both components must act simultaneously. During the independence assumption, the probabilities are multiplied: \(0.99\cdot 0.99=0.9801\). A serial dependence requirement is not the same as reserve capacity.

prompt: A service has two independent replicas. Each works with probability 0.99, one working replica is enough, and error detection and switch is assumed to be perfect. What is the availability of the service in this model?
explanation: Service is down only if both are down. It happens with probability \(0.01\cdot 0.01=0.0001\). Therefore, the availability is \(1-0.0001=0.9999\). The assumptions exclude common errors and conversion problems.

prompt: Two cloud solutions with the same total downtime per month may have different ability to run a long job without interruption.
explanation: One long event and many short events can result in the same total downtime. The pattern of events affects the likelihood of continuous, uninterruptible driving, which is something different from the proportion of time available.

prompt: A database replicates all changes immediately into a reserve, including incorrect deletions. What can a separate, older backup contribute to in such a deletion?

options.text: That deletion never reaches primary database
That incorrect data automatically gets correct only because they have two copies
That reserve capacity alone replaces all recovery planning
Restore to a state before deletion

explanation: A replica can copy the same logical error. A preserved copy before the event provides another restore point. The amount of data that can be lost depends on the time and the recovery system.

prompt: A direct interconnection network shall connect to 48 calculation nodes. Each switch has space for exact 3 calculation nodes, as well as the ports used between the switch. How many such suites are needed at least?
explanation: If each switch serves three compute nodes, \(\frac{48}{3}=16\) switches are needed. In this bristling model, multiple compute nodes share a switch, and inter-switch ports are excluded from the count of three.

prompt: A network has 16 nodes with injection capacity \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) each. A balanced average has four links on \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) in each direction. All eight nodes on the left hand side send only to the right hand side. What is the upper limit over the cut from left to right, and is this full secondary aspect bandwidth relative to the nodes injection?

options.text: \(40\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\); yes, number of nodes does not matter
\(80\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\); yes, both directions can be summed for the same data path
\(160\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\); yes, all nodes are counted on both sides

explanation: One direction over the average is \(4\cdot 10=40\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\). Eight sending nodes can inject \(8\cdot 10=80\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\), so the average cannot carry the entire load at the same time.

prompt: A 2D-mesh uses dimension-order routing: first, the \(x\) coordinates change to the target \(x\), then \(y\). A packet must be from \((0,\,0)\) to \((2,\,1)\). Which of these paths follows the rule?
explanation: The specified \(x\) pre-\(y\) rule completes both \(x\) jumps before the \(y\) jump. The other two three-hop paths change dimension too early; the diagonal jump is not found in this messy.

prompt: Any physical cycle in a connecting network means that the packets in the network are currently locked in a deadlock.
explanation: Deadlock is about dependencies: packets hold resources and wait for other resources in a cycle. Route and resource rules can prevent such dependence even if the physical topology has cycles.

prompt: Four equal packets are kept in separate buffers. Each waits for the next buffer in a closed cycle, and no one can release its buffer until it can proceed. The recovery rule is to remove one packet and re-inject it later. What does the removal get first?

options.text: It breaks at least one of the circular resource dependencies
It makes all the paths shorter in number of jumps
It guarantees that no packet must ever wait again
It automatically increases the physical link capacity

explanation: When one packet releases its resources, another packet in the cycle can acquire the resource it needs. This is abort-and-retry recovery, which differs from preventing deadlock in advance.

prompt: A credit-based sender has zero credits while its link is idle. What does this mean?

options.text: The free link proves that all outstanding data was delivered.
The link is free, but no receiver-buffer credit permits transmission.
The free link permits transmission even when no credits remain.
The absence of credits proves that the receiving device has failed.

explanation: Credits represent permission backed by receiver buffer resources. An idle physical link does not establish that the sender has buffer space reserved at the receiver.

prompt: An ingress-PE adds packets from two different IP prefixes to the same LSP because they should receive the same forward processing. Is such an FEC grouping possible in the lecture model?

options.text: No, an FEC must always correspond exactly to one single IP address
No, packets of the same FEC must have identical payload
Yes, an FEC may group different packets to be treated equally
Only if all label values are the same on each jump

explanation: The FEC indicates the re-dispatching equivalence, not identical content. The lecture shows several possible groupings, including groups of addresses and VPN locations. Therefore, the Ingress policy can bring together several prefixes during appropriate joint processing.

prompt: Two customers have overlapping IP addresses, and the PE routes have to be able to make different IP route listings for them. What mechanism provides separate routing and forwarding contexts on the PE?

options.text: A common global routing table without customer context
One common default route to replace all customer prefixes
Identical route import into one common table for all customers

explanation: A VRF provides its own routing and forwarding context. It's the context that lets the same customer prefix get different meaning; a larger packet or checksum doesn't create such separation.

prompt: Two core switches can use different local MPLS label values for the same FEC, provided their label bindings and forwarding rules are consistent.
explanation: MPLS is based on label bindings and operations as swaps between neighbours. Therefore, the label value does not need to be one global, unchanging identifier throughout the path.

prompt: Someone claims that QUIC’s use of UDP prevents retransmission on reliable QUIC streams. What is wrong with this claim?

options.text: Only IP is permitted to implement retransmission over a datagram service.
QUIC can implement reliability above UDP's unreliable datagram service.
UDP automatically retransmits lost packets when it carries QUIC traffic.
HTTP/3 reliability comes from a TCP connection hidden inside each packet.

explanation: UDP offers an unreliable datagram service. QUIC implements acknowledgment, loss recovery and reliable stream delivery above that service.

prompt: If all necessary QUIC data for stream B have been received but the application requires a result from stream A before B can be used, A may continue to delay the application's use of B.
explanation: Independent transport delivery does not remove dependencies that the application itself has. QUIC can avoid TCP inter-flow blocking without making all application operations independent.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 74–75

prompt: A campus needs at least \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) even when one uplink falls out. Option A has one 40-Gbit/s-uplink; option B has two independent 10-Gbit/s-uplinks. Both are in the budget. Which choice meets the declared error requirement, if other errors are kept outside the model?

options.text: A, because \(40\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) before the error compensates for zero afterwards
Both, because the capacity without errors is at least \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)
None, because every uplink needs \(20\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) to give \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) on error
B, because one remaining uplink still returns \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)

explanation: The requirement concerns capacity after a specific failure. A loses its uplink in that failure, while B retains one 10-Gbit/s link. Normal capacity and capacity after failure are distinct.
source: Networking in the Real World · PDF page 8
